text.p: General Electric Co is on track to sharply boost revenue and earnings growth rates in its industrial and consumer products businesses, say Wall Street analysts -- who expect an increase in the dividend, a stock split and a sharply higher stock price by the year 2000.
"There's an awful lot of upside in that stock over the next two to three years," said Nicholas Heymann, analyst at NatWest Securities. He expects GE's stock to double in three years.
General Electric's stock is already one of the better performers of 1996. With the price at 102-1/2 at midday Tuesday, the shares are up 30-1/2 or 42 percent since the beginning of the year.
That handily tops the gain of about 27 percent in the Dow industrials so far this year and about 23 percent in the Standard & Poor's 500. General Electric is a component of both market barometers.
GE's stock gain so far in 1996 follows a rise of 41 percent during the course of 1995.
Heymann says while several internal programs at General Electric are aimed at widening margins, the key is revenue growth. "The top line is going to be where the explosion is," he said.

Analyst Michael Linsky of McDonald & Co said recently he expects the company to announce later this month an increase in the quarterly dividend on common stock to about $0.52 per share from the current $0.46. He also expects an extension of the share repurchase program and a stock split.
A spokesman for GE declined to comment, citing corporate policy not to make pre-announcements of such moves.

Several analysts said a dividend increase would be no big surprise because General Electric has raised its dividend each year for 20 consecutive years. The last increase was announced in December 1995.

Analyst Kent Newcomb of A.G. Edwards & Sons said he expects GE's earnings to continue growing at a 10 percent-plus rate. He expects operating earnings of $4.40 per share this year and $4.95 in 1996. He said the company's plastics business is very strong and National Broadcasting Co (NBC) is a standout.
On Monday, Nielsen Media Research said NBC maintained its lead over its network television rivals in the November ratings period.

Heymann said a key his bullish outlook is an acceleration of revenue growth in the base businesses, excluding the GE Capital Services unit, to around 8.9 percent per year between 1996 and 2000. That compares with about 3.9 percent in the early 1990s. For the company overall, with Capital Services, revenue growth should average close to 12 percent per year in the next few years, the analyst said.

Operating profit should have a 14.7 compounded annual growth rate over the next few years, including GE Capital Services, Heymann said. In the base business, excluding GE Capital Services, operating profits are likely to grow at 12.4 percent (corrects from 11.7 percent) per year compounded, he said.

Asked how he expects GE to pull off this significant increase in revenues and operating profit growth rates, Heymann cited globalization of the company's businesses, emphasis on revenue from servicing in such areas as jet engines, locomotives and medical equipment, and a program known within the company as Six Sigma.
Six Sigma is aimed at dramatically lowering error rates.

A GE spokesman said Six Sigma uses methods such as identificaton of "critical to quality" elements in a process to trace any errors that might get through and prevent recurrences. Heymann said such programs can have dramatic
effect on the bottom line.

As analysts ponder where GE is going to be in the year 2000, an often-asked question is what will happen when chairman and chief executive Jack Welch turns over the reins to a successor. Welch, who recently turned 61, has signalled he will step down at the mandatory retirement age of 65.
The company has a succession plan although it declines to discuss details, a spokesman said. Analysts point out there is no shortage of talented managers at the company.

Another often-asked question is how the company would fare in a recession. Newcomb said GE has been able to grow earnings through a number of recessions. He notes the company is not overly-concentrated in any one industry. Furthermore, he does not expect a recession.
